utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently the technician tells us they're not quite sure where the problem is coming from. Will you please try and give us the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I will try to do so, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Kyle Wood, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Can we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us have the appearances for the other Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids good morning to all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as the staff in this courtroom. Today we will complete the testimony of the expert witness, which absolutely has to be completed today. We hope that the time that will be given to the Prosecution and for the questions of the Judges and any observations by the Defence will allow us to finish the hearing at a quarter to 2.00. Should we finish earlier, we could in that case address the outstanding issues; that is, the five documents that Mr. Bourgon has to present, and the famous category of Mr. Dixon, which will also be the subject of a presentation, but that is, of course, on condition that we complete the testimony before we are due to adjourn. Madam Usher, could you go and fetch the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Let me check first that you are hearing the interpretation of my words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I hear you loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As you know, today is the last day of your testimony. You have spent a whole week in The Hague. But lest assured, we have taken steps so that the hearing will be finished by 13.45 on the outside. Normally it would be the turn of the Prosecution to ask you questions on the basis of the cross-examination of the Defence, and at the end of that stage, if there is no response from the Defence, the three Judges in front of you will also have questions for you. So, Mr. Mundis, without further delay, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, based on the documents you've reviewed, including any material that was shown to you by the Defence, can you please comment on the operational tempo with respect to combat within the 3rd Corps AOR throughout 1993.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to, because it's -- it's difficult, since I only concentrated on those events which we are concerned of. I didn't look into the overall campaign, and I must tell you that I didn't participate so much in the overall campaign. But one thing is clear: There was not constant war. There was not a constant campaign. There were short periods of military operations and long pauses in between, and then the fighting broke up again. So within that fighting phases, the tempo, I think, was very high, but then it was reduced, not to normality because the animosities were still going on. But it was not a constant military battle one has to perceive here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, in light of that response, can you tell us how that operational tempo affected the ability of a commander to investigate alleged crimes and/or refer alleged crimes to the appropriate legal institutions.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the appropriate legal institutions were not constantly involved in the military operations, so they were even during the military operations free to investigate and do their legal obligations. Besides that, the commanders who were very busy during the operations in executing and controlling the -- the pursuit of the operations were capable of turning their attention to those things which they could not fulfil during the operations. And one of those things are their legal obligations, investigations, and so on. So yes, they had the chance to do that in those pauses I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, you told us, I believe it was either yesterday or perhaps the day before, or even both of those days, that President Izetbegovic placed great importance on adherence to international humanitarian law. What impact, if any, would you expect such presidential direction or guidance to have on commanders who became aware of possible violations of that law by their soldiers or those under their effective control?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the commanders had to adhere to the legal obligations as they have been laid down in the legal obligations of the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the laws of the Republic of Yugoslavia as far as they were adhered by the Bosnian forces. This is one thing. The other thing is that this law was, I think, as every law, very binding, in that you were obliged as a military commander of the forces fighting in that area to make sure that your soldiers also prevented from -- being prevented from breaking that law. And if they did, you had to investigate why they did and had to do everything in order to prevent further breaking of the international law. So this was, on the one hand, a -- a legal obligation, and I think a very strict one, which as we discussed before was, so to speak, the left and the right boundary in which you could operate. On the other hand, the breaking of the law, and especially breaking of the international law and the humanitarian law has a big effect on the discipline and morale of your own forces, so you are also based on this factor very much interested to -- to keep the international law at a very high level and -- and to make sure that your soldiers are really behaving appropriately according to those legal obligations. And you would do everything to prevent them from breaking that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand what you said, General, but my question is a slightly different one. It has to do with the effect of President Izetbegovic's policy, if you will, of requiring adherence to the law of war. What impact, if any, would that have on soldiers or commanders in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have to obey his order. It's a political guideline for the conduct of war for the Bosnian-Herzegovinian -- Bosnia-Herzegovina armed forces, and therefore it is a key element you have to look for, that this has been -- that this has been executed, because this is will of the president, besides being expressed in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, what effect, if any, does the fact that one side to a conflict is in a defensive posture have on the responsibility or ability of a commander to investigate and refer potential violations of the law to the appropriate legal authorities?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it has no effect whatsoever, whether you are in an offensive operation or defensive operation or retrograde operation, the law has to be applied no matter what you are doing in a military operation, so it's notwithstanding what kind of operations you are into.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, yesterday you were asked about the HVO and VRS or Bosnian Serb army being unlawful armies under the domestic law of Bosnia. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What effect, if any, would the fact that the opposing side may have been an unlawful army under domestic law have on the ability or responsibility of a commander to investigate alleged violations of the law?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it doesn't have any effect, because no matter what the enemy is doing, the laws of your country are binding and obliging to you to -- to adhere to the law. So this doesn't -- doesn't have any effect on you as a commander of those Bosnian forces by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, what effect, if any, does the fact that one's opponents have committed war crimes have on the ability of a commander to investigate and refer potential violations of the law committed by his own forces to the appropriate legal authorities?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it doesn't have any effect, rather than the moral effect on your troops. And I think if -- if things happen on -- on the other side, the more you are obliged to prevent things on your side; otherwise, you come into a spiral of violence on either side where both sides basically are breaking the rules of international law which will effect your own soldiers in a very detrimental way. So I think you again, if the enemy commits atrocities, you are not allowed to -- to answer in the same way or just to -- to basically commit revenge on that. This is inlawful or unlawful and you're not -- you're not allowed and you better don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Reinhardt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no further questions in re-examination. However, before I sit down, the Prosecution would ask that the documents which have been marked as DH documents for identification - and I'm specifically referring to DH154 for identification through DH163 for identification; that is, the first ten tabs of the two binders that were produced - the Prosecution, Mr. President, is asking that these documents be admitted into evidence and be renumbered as Prosecution exhibits. The Prosecution does this because we believe that these documents are helpful to the Trial Chamber; we believe that these documents are of assistance to the Trial Chamber in its important task of determining exactly what happened. Although the Defence have indicated that they at some point intend on tendering those documents, the time frame in which they are intending to do that is unclear to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution believes that these documents should be put into evidence so that Your Honours may have the fullest possible picture as to events occurring both within the 3rd Corps and within the legal institutions that were operating in the area at the relevant time periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're asking that DH154 to 163 should be admitted into evidence, though they were marked for identification by the Defence, because you feel that they should be tendered and that they are admissible. However, I want to ask you about the report of the expert witness, the written report. Are you asking that it be admitted? Shall we give it a number? I think it's already been done. Is that right? Mr. Registrar, what number do we have for the report of the expert witness? Apparently it is P108; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can confirm that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I'm looking at the Defence. There are two issues here: Normally when there is re-examination by the Prosecution after the cross-examination of an expert witness, the usage was not to have additional questions except if the Chamber allows it exceptionally, believing that it is of special importance. Therefore, does the Defence have any additional questions for this witness in view of the answers given during the re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence does not wish to ask the expert witness any additional questions. On the other hand, we might have questions to put following the questions of the Chamber. But at this stage, we have no specific reason to ask for special permission to put additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the second issue of the documents, DH154 to 163, the Prosecution wants those documents to be admitted into evidence. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our view, a number of these documents cannot be admitted into evidence for the reasons that we set out during the debate on the admissibility of documents proposed by the Prosecution. Our intention was to have them marked for identification so that when we call witnesses or when we hear future witnesses, we can pick up those documents that have already been identified and in this way facilitate our proceedings. However, what we are saying this morning is that because the Prosecution agrees to the admission of certain documents, this should not diminish the argument that we presented, because we feel that many of those documents are in the same position as documents to which we objected and for which we believe a witness will be required. But if there is mutual agreement, then we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will deliberate during the break and give you our ruling. We can now pass on to the stage of Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Reinhardt, there are three Judges in front of you, and as I do not wish to monopolise the proceedings, I will give the floor to the Judge on my right, then the Judge on my left, and I will be the last

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. General, having reviewed the document provided to you by the Prosecution, could you tell us whether General Hadzihasanovic was aware that civilians were detained in various detention centres and did he take steps to have them liberated.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember that there were reports about civilians detained. I don't remember having read any document on any specific case in which he basically interfered for liberating those, but he had issued a lot of orders to his subordinate commands preventing them from doing that. I mean, from -- from detaining civilians in -- in some of their installations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you don't know whether he issued orders to the wardens of those penitentiaries to have civilian detainees freed.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, not that I'm aware of. I -- I just don't remember any of -- of those particular documents. I don't think I have seen one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were General Hadzihasanovic and General Kubura aware of the bad treatment that these detainees were subjected to in the detention centres that were in the area of responsibility of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on the orders given by General Hadzihasanovic to his subordinate commands to treat the civilian population according to the international law and to prevent them from detaining people, I would conclude from that that he must have had some -- some evidence that there was not all -- that this was not always the case. But as I have said before, I don't remember any particular document expressing this to a certain particular case. They were all very general in -- in their -- in their contents, not related to a particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I'm going a little fast. But we've come to the end of your testimony. Do you stand by the conclusions that you expressed in your expert paper?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I already tried to indicate yesterday, having seen so many additional documents which prove that General Hadzihasanovic did not only issue orders but also went through the whole circle of making sure that the perpetrators were treated legally according to the law, I would change, and I have changed my attitude, saying that he only initiated the first step and didn't do the other steps. Obviously he did this. Where I still have some problems is the question of the adherence or the inclusion of Mujahedin in the military organisation of especially the 7th Mountain Brigade. I think the evidence which I have put down in my paper and which I discussed here shows that the cooperation was much closer and much more detail -- detailed than the Defence thought it was, and therefore I think once you plan and execute operations against an enemy and if you include, no matter what kind of forces they are - in this case, the Mujahedin - in your operations, you also take responsibility for the conduct of those forces who were under your command during that particular time, and in this regard I haven't changed my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RASOAZANANY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judge who is sitting to my left also has some questions he would like to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When you came here this Monday, I had a long list of questions, and most of these questions have been asked -- have been answered by you in a very clear and convincing way, and I'm grateful for that. I still have two sets of questions to put to you, first on the treatment of prisoners; and secondly, on the situation of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, regarding the treatment of prisoners, you have not written much in your report. In fact, you have hardly mentioned the topic at all, I think. Was there any special reason for it not to deal with that topic specifically?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The reason is that based on the document provided to me, the question of -- particular question and particular cases of handling the prisoners of war was not a case. The key case I looked into was Miletici, where HVO soldiers who have surrendered have been killed afterwards. But the overall question of prisoners came up only in two additional -- in the documents I remember, in two additional cases, where General Hadzihasanovic on one hand and the 7th Mountain Brigade, on the other hand, asked for the -- for the exchange of prisoners whom they called soldiers, and they were actually Mujahedin. So taking care of prisoners and trying to get them back on your own side, saying these are soldiers and getting to the other side and say, "We want to have them back," and naming them, and telling the names and the country they were coming from, also shows some kind of responsibility towards those soldiers who became prisoners on the other side, i.e., by the HVO. Besides that, sir, the question of handling of prisoners and exchange of prisoners was not a very concrete one besides - I come back to what I told the Madam Judge before - besides in those general orders by General Hadzihasanovic and also by General Kubura that they should treat prisoners according to the international law. But this was very general, not specified on a specific case, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, since you did not write explicitly about that matter, I'm not going to ask you questions on the basis of the least facts or the documents of the case, but I'm interested in your opinion as a commander with regard to the treatment of prisoners in general, and I hope you are able to tell me a few things about the responsibilities of commanders in general, in the abstract, so to say.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the legal obligations for a commander to take care of the well-being of prisoners is based on -- on two major factors: One is the legal obligation by the international law that prisoners have to be treated according to the international law and The Hague Convention. And I think he has to train his soldiers, to teach his soldiers that they know what they're up to. This is to take care of the prisoners he is making. On the other hand, you have to teach your soldiers how they have to behave once they become prisoners. And I think the biggest protection for your own soldiers once they become prisoners is that you treat your opponent's prisoners the appropriate way, because if you don't do that, you might have repercussions on your own soldiers, which you want to prevent. So to keep the international law, as far as the treatment of prisoners is concerned, according to the law is a key thing, I think, also for the morale and the protection of your own soldiers. So it's in my interest as a commander to do everything to treat my opponent prisoners the best way possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's take the matter step by step, then. First of all, I do not want to -- to put to you leading questions or to act as a demagogue or whatever, but would you agree with me that prisoners of war and civilian prisoners are a very vulnerable category of persons in a battle situation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And why would you think that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they are left to your will. They are left also to the power you have over them. And you can mistreat them and you can treat them the appropriate way. And they have no chance to do something about it because they have delivered themselves to -- to me in this regard and to my will to treat them accordingly or against them. So they have no chance to fight. They have no chance to defend themselves. The only chance they have is maybe a visit by some people of the Red Cross, and this is not very helpful either. So once you become a prisoner of war and once you believe you are treated accordingly to the rules of the international law, I think it's -- it's just fair from the commander's point of view that this prisoner, then, has been treated accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I would like to review briefly with you the factors that may make a prisoner vulnerable. I can imagine that one factor would be that prisoners could be exposed to the wrath of the guardians or the wrath of the army, desires of revenge, of retaliation, and that this would provoke more easily physical violence than in normal prison situations. Is that a factor of significance?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a factor. And we just see it in the real world how much a factor this is. And I think this is one of the reasons, sir, that you have also to train your wardens taking care of those prisoners, that they know their legal obligations and that they don't extend their power over those prisoners of war who cannot defend themselves any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you are in fact saying that once you have an untrained army or a badly trained army or a not sufficiently trained army, that increases the chances of ill-treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. May I give you an example of what I mean by that? When I was the commander in Kosovo, we have no prisons, because all prisons have been destroyed by the international air force. So I remember that my German soldiers in prison had built up a prison with military police which was not prepared for that job, and I just disbanded the prison because I did not want to put my soldiers and jeopardise doing something wrong towards the guys they had in prison. So I think you really have to make sure that those who have -- who are given the mission to take care of their inmates are well-trained and know how to do this; otherwise, misdeeds are due.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Another factor that could be important - but I'm asking your opinion about it - is the following: The conflict in Bosnia in 1993 had elements of an inter-racial or inter-religious conflict. Are these circumstances that increases the chances of prisoners being ill-treated?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think civil wars like the one we have encountered in Bosnia and other places are more revengeful and more bloody and -- against the war than a normal war, because many people have known each other. Sometimes people who lived in the same village were fighting each other, and they were not only fighting for the military objectives but sometimes also for their own objectives, fighting out things which have been there for years. And I saw this all over in the Balkans again and again, how bloody this fight was, and I think it was more atrocious than you would normally believe a war would going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So we have now reviewed three different factors that may explain the vulnerability of prisoners in general or in a specific conflict. Could you add other factors that are relevant in this respect?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I'd like to have your opinion in general on the responsibility of commanders with regard to -- to prisoners taken, and I also have a number of specific questions on that. First, I would like to invite you to -- as a commander yourself, based on your experience and your knowledge, what exactly should a commander do when his troops take enemy soldiers as prisoners or civilians as prisoners? What -- could you give a short impression of the responsibilities of the commander in that field?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'll try. I never did it myself, because I never had prisoners or -- or prisoners of war. But I think it really starts very early once you take the first prisoners that you check back with those commanders who have taken those prisoners and make sure that they know how to deal with the prisoners and to make sure that they do the utmost that the prisoners are not being mishandled. As I said before, otherwise you might have a spiralling effect in a very negative way, which might then affect your own forces. So as a commander, I would look and talk to the commander on the ground by telephone, by radio, whatsoever, to make sure that the appropriate measures are being taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you would not wait the moment of becoming active -- you would not await complaints before becoming active?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there is a kind of prevention and precaution which is a very sensitive one in that particular case. And as I said, it has a big effect on my own soldiers, on -- on the morale of my own soldiers. If they know that prisoners are being taken care of appropriately, because then they also can expect the same will happen to them. Therefore, I think it's a very key question for the morale. And again and again during this testimony I tried to -- to say how important the morale for the soldiers -- of the soldiers are for -- for the success I have as a commander. Therefore, I would in a kind of a preventive mode try to -- not try. I would call the commander on the ground and tell him again how important it is that the first prisoners of war and the following ones are treated according to the law. Once the things have been -- gone in the wrong direction, the propaganda effect which will be the consequence of this can almost never be settled again. It's out. The ghost is out of the bottle. So you have to prevent this from the very first beginning that this will not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So in effect you are taking an outspoken proactive attitude in this manner.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me put to you some specific questions on proactive approach of protection of prisoners. Would a normal commander, or would you as a commander insist on knowing the numbers, the identity, the places where prisoners are kept?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would not know all the -- the places and the numbers, depending, sir, on the rank of commander. If it's in my battalion, if I'm a battalion commander and that happens within my battalion, I would be very interested how it happened, where it happened, but I'm not so much interested in the identity. Maybe I will have to interrogate some of them to know what's going on on the other side. And I would also be very interested where they are being held as prisoners of war afterwards. But normally, again, sir, you prepare this; you don't go in the battle unprepared for treating prisoners of war, because you know that happens, so you have to -- you have to look for that, that you have some installations in which you can put them. And the mission, the obligations of the commander would be to do this beforehand and not once you have a large group of prisoners of war you cannot deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would you, in the second place, would you create a system of -- of reporting, with regard to prisoners? Would you insist on receiving reports every week or every now and then on where prisoners are held, how are they being treated, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, it depends on what level you are commanding, I think, and not every level would deal into that. But as the commander responsible for keeping those prisoners, yes, sir, I would have that, and I would have regular reports and I probably also would regularly go to those prisons and watch them themselves, because talking to the prisoners is a key factor also of -- of making sure that what you know is reported is true, because we talked about the last day about reports. One thing, sir, is absolutely true: About 50 to 60 per cent of the reports, the contents of the reports you are getting, are somehow coloured. I mean, they are being put in a positive way for them who are reporting. If you don't go on investigating, as we saw investigating teams checking the area of the 3rd Corps -- if you don't go there by yourself and see by your own eyes and talk to the people, you only get 50 per cent of the truth. So you would do that. And I think as the highest commander in this regard, I would get regular reports not on a daily basis but regular summary -- summary reports about the situation of the prisoners of war in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you proceeded already my next question, that was if you would institute a -- a system of inspection or if you would go yourself or your deputy or whatever person you might make use of, and your answer is in the affirmative, yes, that was an important aspect of preventing and also of repressing crimes against prisoners.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Coming back to my own experience. In Kosovo the only prison which we had was an American prison in Camp Bondsteel, as it was called, and I went there about once a month unannounced, just to come in and look what the conditions were and to talk to the inmates, which were not prisoners of war - which were criminals - but nevertheless, this was at the end the only prison I had, and it was very important for me to see with my own eyes about the situation, but also to make sure that the wardens knew that I would be there at any moment checking what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would you agree with me or what is your opinion on the following question: Is there a duty for the commander in general to anticipate possible criminal behaviour of his troops against prisoners?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is a very, very difficult question, because it is concerned with your trust in the human being of your subordinates. We all know that in wars powers are being set free in the human being which are normally somehow covered by your cultural, religious background, and therefore I think you are better to do something about this than trusting that everything goes according to the law and according to the regulations. In this regard, I would not trust anybody on the long run, and I think you have to do -- and to provide preventive measures and protective measures that this would not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And this, you are saying, for all armed conflicts in which prisoners are taken?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, sir, this is the part of the human being, and we see that in every country, and notwithstanding the cultural level, you find people, once they get the power that they mistreat other people. I don't know why they do that, but it seems that this is obvious, and notwithstanding their educational level that people do that. Knowing that and having been exposed to things like that, I lost my trust in this regard, and I would do everything again and again to make sure that those underdogs of the war - and these are the prisoners of war - are being treated accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This is about prisoners of war in general and civilian prisoners in general. Are there circumstances in the case of Bosnia - we have already discussed this a little bit - that make the responsibility of a commander even more pressing or more important in this field? I mentioned the inter-racial or inter-religious character, civil war aspects you mentioned. We have briefly discussed the inexperience of troops, new soldiers. Are these factors that also increase, so to speak, the responsibility of a commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think it increases his responsibility, and the commander knows about the situation because he has the overall knowledge of what was going on in his area of responsibility, and therefore the commander would do the utmost and take every measure possible under -- in his effective command and control capabilities to prevent things from happening. If -- if you have soldiers who are not adequately treated, if you have a situation in which ethnic groups clash with each other, besides fighting each other at military -- as military, the violence is normally, as I said before, higher, the atrocities tend to become more aggressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, the treatment of prisoners may in some situations be a matter for the army but also for other persons outside the army. And I also have some questions on that matter. Sometimes it seems Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the responsibility for the treatment of prisoners is shared among different institutions or different groups of persons. My main question or my most general question is the following: Once you have taken prisoners as an army, I'm inclined to think - but please contradict me if I'm mistaken - but my assumption would be that your responsibility as a commander exists as long as they are prisoners, or is there a moment in time where you may transfer your responsibility to -- to other instances, other persons?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, prisoner of war is always a burden to a military commander, because you have to guard him, you have to feed him, and your main job is not to guard prisoners; your main job is to fight. So everybody who is preventing you from fighting, because you have to take care of him, is a burden. And I think this is sometimes also the reason why prisoners of war, once -- or soldiers, once they have surrendered, are being killed, because people realise they become a burden afterwards, even so it's illegal. So as a commander, I would do the utmost to transfer those prisoners in any other authority -- to any other authority, the internal authority of my country, who could take care of them, who would have wardens, who would have -- probably also have prisons, so that I would be relieved. So my mission would be to keep the prisoners, to treat them, to -- to see, to identify them, and then move them appropriately into some civil detention facilities. The earlier the better for me, because then I can concentrate on my main mission again, and the main mission is fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And once this has happened, your responsibility as a commander is --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it turns then to the ones who take the prisoners over from me, and that ends my responsibility towards them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And does it make any difference whether these authorities are within your area of responsibility geographically speaking, or not?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if these are civilian responsibilities -- civilian organisations, then it's not my responsibility any more, as I am not responsible for the civil police or the -- the judges or whoever is working in my area of responsibility. I just transfer this to them. And whatever happens in the civilian field is not my responsibility as a commander, as long as I'm not the military governor of that area and all these things are under my command, which was not in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yesterday you said in a different context, and that's why I'm putting the question also: If civilians do not react to crime in your own area of responsibility, you have to do it. But that is apparently something that does not apply to this situation.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said yesterday that if there are criminal activities going on - and I referred yesterday to the Mujahedin - and if the civil authorities are not willing to do something about this and if war crimes are committed by these Mujahedin, I think I have to do something about it. I have to -- I have different possibilities. I can go to the civil authorities and insist that they do something. And if they don't have the power to do this, I will do it in accordance -- and in concordance for them, but you just cannot leave it open because this will create a very adverse situation in my area of responsibility. This is what I was saying yesterday and what I'm saying today too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If prisoners are held in an institution - let's say a school or another building of civilian origin with normally civilian authorities managing these establishments - but if the prisoner is held in such institutions and the guardians are in fact members of your own army, what would you consider to be your responsibility as a commander in that situation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it might happen very often that the prisoners are being held in infrastructure which is not the normal infrastructure for detention, because you have no other ones, so you have to keep them. And if you can get them in a school, this is already a -- a big step forward, because they are not exposed to wind and rain and snow, so they have a roof over their head, and they are living under normal conditions besides -- I would not call it maybe "normal positions" but improved positions and most of the time in better positions than they lived before while they were soldiers, living out in the trenches. My responsibility would be that they are provided food, that they are provided medical care, that they are provided the assistance they need, and that the wardens taking care of them treat them appropriately. I think this would be my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And if the wardens were members of your own troops, you would still retain your power of -- of disciplining or punishing your soldiers.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this would be a normal case, that they are under my disciplinary command. And if they misbehave, I can take the whole variety of disciplinary measures against them, and you would probably do that, being a commander, if they don't do their job appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the fact that you have that power also obliges you to take preventive measures.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the soldiers knowing I have that power is a preventive measure by itself. Because they know if they misbehave, they might be up to some disciplinary consequences. On the other hand, if this doesn't help and if they misbehave, I would use my disciplinary power, making sure that they're either -- either relieved and other soldiers are coming in or that they are disciplinary taken care of in the way that they not do this any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to put to you some questions on a topic that we have been discussing for the last few days, the situation of the Mujahedin. You have written about that in your report. There have been a lot of questions being put to you in the past few days. I have some questions that may or may not precede the questions that have been put to you, and I would like to submit them to you --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: -- and I would like to hear your answer on that. There was a situation in 1993 in Bosnia in which the commander, either of the 3rd Corps or another part of the army, had, so to speak, territorial command and -- and operational command, if I am correctly summarising the discussion. There were two aspects of -- of the situation of a commander: He had a command over a certain area, his area of responsibility; and he had an operational command. Am I correct in summarising the situation in this way?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But it's very difficult to differentiate what is a territorial and what is an operational command. Having been a territorial and an operational commander, I must tell you once you have an area of operations in which you concentrate all your forces available to you to fight the battle, you are the operational commanders and those territorial forces then are part of your operational forces and under your responsibility, notwithstanding whether they are operational army, territorial army, whatever you have. The problem is that there was the territorial army first and the other forces then joined them. But all together they formed the 3rd Corps. And even those 14 municipal defensive councils were part of the 3rd Corps, notwithstanding how they called themselves. So this distinction really doesn't matter for the operations and for the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If you talk in your report about area of responsibility, then I'm inclined to think that you refer to a geographical aspect.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, if in your area of responsibility there are soldiers of foreign origin, if these soldiers are prepared to fight for the same cause as you yourself are fighting for but -- and if, on the other hand, they are unwilling to be placed fully under your command but prefer to have a rather loose horizontal relationship with you and your troops, then that would be an awkward situation, I presume, for a commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is a very bad situation, because as we discussed it before, unity of command in an area of responsibility is a key factor. And whatever happens there during military operations will affect your responsibility as a commander and it will be credited to you. And if something doesn't go according to the way you want to fight the battle and if these are the forces who are doing things against your interest of -- in the operations, then it's you who have to put up with that. Therefore, you would do everything trying to clear this mess in order to have unity of command and with this a clear-cut responsibility in the hierarchical form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if you are faced with this situation, when assuming command the first thing you would do is to try to stop this situation as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. To stop or to solve it. It might be that there's a possibility to solve it, rather than stopping it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So your choice might be either to force them to accept your command fully and permanently or to force them to leave your area of responsibility, or is that too --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think this is very well put. These are the alternatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: These are the alternatives. And if you don't do that as a commander, if you accept the presence of the fighting forces in your area of responsibility, you in fact accept also their presence as fighting forces.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my understanding, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: From which you profit as a -- as an army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have probably seen the report of the 7th Brigade in which they say the circumstances that the Mujahedin are fighting as advanced forces for the old forces is a booster for the morale, and they're very happy to have those Arabs and Turks fighting with them, because it increases the morale of their own soldiers. So you see how close this relation must have been. And coming back to what you just have said, I only can subscribe -- subscribe to your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I don't know for certain whether these Arabs you mention now or these Turks were part of the 7th Brigade or were outside, so I'll leave that as it may be. But my next question is the following: If you accept presence of forces that are not fully integrated in your army, without forcing them to accept your command fully and permanently, do you also accept by acquiescing to the situation, do you also accept or assume responsibilities for their acts and conduct, especially or even in situations in which they would take independent action that you have not ordered or in any way promoted?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is my understanding of the situation. But I -- I just wanted to say that the command of the 3rd Corps tried to solve this situation but it took a while until they solved it, and at the end I think they solved it by institutionalising this unit as the El Mujahedin Detachment, but it took a while. And until that time, it's exactly as you said; you just have a tacit understanding that you don't look too much into that and you basically accept it as it is, maybe because you don't feel that you can do something. We heard yesterday that they were talking -- that General Hadzihasanovic was talking about he doesn't want to open up a third front, which might have been, if he had done something about this, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There's an objection to my question, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No, it is certainly not an objection to your question. It's simply for a point of clarification. The two or three last questions that were put to the witness, I didn't quite understand whether the question referred to a legal obligation, a moral obligation, or a military obligation, because the has been prompted to ask -- to discuss a number of issues. But I would like to know in what light he's providing his answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to my line of questioning. But I'm trying to -- to establish firstly the -- the responsibility of a commander in general for troops that are not integrated within his army. And once I have received answers on that, I would like to put questions in terms of criminal responsibility. But I'm not yet that far, I must say. But it will come. Don't be disturbed. So my question is, General, to -- and you have already answered. It was a general question: If you in your area of responsibility are confronted with forces that are not integrated in your command, that have a sort of independent existence, and you acquiesce in that situation, this may create forms of responsibility for what they are doing, even if they act outside, do things that you have not ordered or do not follow from your orders or whatever.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And the next question that I would have is the same: Does it also engage your criminal responsibility if they commit within their activities, within their independent activities certain crimes? Does that make you also -- does that also create an obligation for you to -- to intervene, in terms of punishment, of investigations, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you address this question to me personally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a German -- as a German commander, I would be responsible, criminally accountable for everything which happens and to -- in my area of responsibility. And I think this is applicable to almost all NATO countries, as far as I know. I was responsible for everything which happened in my area of responsibility and I had to take actions accordingly. Now, in that particular case we're discussing, I thought that some of the rules which were deducted or applied from the JNA forces, especially the rules of applying the international law in which it says the commander is responsible for everything in his area of responsibility, I was told by the defence that this was not applicable to the Bosnian forces and I -- maybe I did not -- not maybe. I just did not know this. I thought it was applicable like other things as well. So I cannot tell you in a paragraph or article whether this applies in the same way to the Bosnian forces. For my forces, it would be an absolute must.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You are right that there are, of course, a number of questions of a legal nature involved here in this problem and in the back of -- on the background, and we're all aware of these questions. But I'm -- I'm not asking you for a legal opinion. I'm asking you your view as a -- an experienced commander. What would you do? What would you think your obligations were.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And maybe if you underestimate or overestimate your responsibilities in legal terms, that is not -- not something that I am interested in in this moment.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if you have troops which lead a rather independent existence but find themselves in your area of responsibility, you said, "I would have a responsibility to repress crimes that have been committed by them."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The other aspect is that if you accept a situation, you are not in a position to -- to take preventive measures, or are you? In the field of preventing crime.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it's very difficult. I think the only prevention you really have in this regard is that you order your troops, who are cooperating with these freelance forces, that they do the utmost, that those troops are in accordance to the -- in accordance to the law. And if they don't do, that you take actions accordingly in order to -- to punish them and to prevent them from continuing to do what they have done before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if I may resume your point of view. It doesn't really matter so much whether legally speaking or criminally -- in terms of criminal law speaking, whether the Mujahedin were a part of a certain brigade or a certain corps or a certain battalion or were acting independently from them. What -- what would be the differences, in terms of responsibility of the commander to prevent and to punish?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prevent them in either case, sir, because as I said, this would effect my operations the way they do their -- their way of operating. And whether they are included as organic elements in some of my units -- by elements, by individuals -- or whether they do it as freelance, the consequences of the criminal activities of them are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for your answers, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said that you had a series of questions to answer and you told us that the Prosecution provided you with numerous documents and that your report was drafted on the basis of those documents. Could you tell the Judges at what point in time you were contacted by the Prosecution and asked to prepare this report. When did this happen, if you remember? Which year and month?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm afraid that I don't have the exact date here. I think it's one and a half years -- about one and a half years ago, and I was contacted first not by the Prosecution but by my Ministry of Defence, giving me the freedom to operate with the ICTY and asking me to support the ICTY in a way I would be addressed to. But it's been about one and a half years ago, but I don't know exactly when it was and I don't have all these papers with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You also told us, answering questions, that you met with the Prosecution and that after that they gave you the documents. In general terms, how much time did you spend? I'm not asking you for the number of days or hours. But in general terms, how much time did you devote to the drafting of your written report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as we have said before, there were a couple of drafts which I put forward, because at the beginning, since this is a total new environment for me, I had just problems to know what I was supposed to do, and therefore I came back to the Prosecution asking them, you know, what exactly they expected me with the material provided to me and having gone through the material and having got a global knowledge what was going on there, how -- what was expected from me. Therefore, I would say I -- I devoted much more time than I anticipated at the beginning to that case, because it was difficult for me to analyse it and it was difficult for me to re-analysing it based on new questions where I had to go through the material again and again and again, just trying to find the appropriate answers through going through the documents, because I had no idea what was the proper answer. I just could deduct the idea out through -- from the documents. And this was a very time-consuming and tedious process, and I also -- I just know that I was always working one or two weeks, depending on the size of the material, in a row, just leaving everything else, in order to know where the documents are, how they would interfere, and how I could put them into a written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In doing this work, did you do it all alone or did you ask other people to help you with their opinions, military people, technicians, specialists? Did you work alone, or as experts do, did you consult other people as well?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know how experts do, because this is my unique experience in that. I've never done before. I was asked to give my opinion as a former general, so I did not refer to anybody else, because I think I only can give them my opinion as a former general, right or wrong. Try the best to make out of it. And the only guy -- the only person I contacted on that was my former translator in my headquarters at Heidelberg, who has to polish my translation in the appropriate way. I think he is the only one who has seen that paper besides myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have explained that you spent weeks looking through the documents.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In looking for information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In looking for information and verification of information, were you prompted to consult documents that were not provided to you by the Prosecution but articles, books, other reports? Were you fishing for information, as they say, so that your opinion could be formed and for you to be able to answer the very specific questions put to you? Did you expand your field of research to include other documents? We know that you're a historian, that you have written about subjects, and you have the practice of judging and assessing documents. So my question is: Did you consult other documents besides those provided to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you satisfied yourself with the documents provided to you by the Prosecution to give your personal opinion without using other documents as verification. Is that what the Chamber should gather from your answer?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes, sir. These were very specific questions pertaining three general officers and in the meantime two general officers, and I think about the questions given to me and the possible answers expected or I had to give could be deducted only from the sources, the documents given by me but by no other material, because they were very specific, with the exception of the command and control relationship, as a commander would have. And you know I -- I took the liberty to -- to deduct this from my German laws just to have a background on that one. But this was the only additional document sources I went to, and these were the -- the German laws, the German military laws and a book on the comparison of the military law within the NATO countries in order to give me a better feeling whether my appreciation of what the commander is responsible for would be similar in the British and the French and other armies in the war -- in NATO, and these were the documents I went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still discussing your CV, you have told us that you held several command positions and in the Balkans and within the territory of ex-Yugoslavia you held command posts so that you are familiar with the territory. So you had the advantage of being active on the ground there, in addition to being a general. The fact that you were active in the Balkans and also in Kosovo, but more particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was the fact that you had a command position there, did that have any effect on your written report, any bearing?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Because by the time I became the national commander of the German forces of UNPROFOR and then IFOR and SFOR had me very often in the country supervising what my troops were doing, but this was after the military operation have ceased between the warring factors. This was in 1994 and the following years. So I might have -- have had a better appreciation of what was going on, depending on the terrain, depending also on all these destructions I have seen, and talking to I don't know how many people in the country about their experience of the war. And we basically have established our headquarters and a former concern of the Bosnian forces, in which both sides were fighting atrociously against each other. So this might have been affected my general appreciation but not the questions that were put forward for me to answer. And if I may -- if I may add, sir, this was one of my first answers to the Prosecution, that I told them I'm not and I'm not willing to become an expert in the operations on the Balkans in that particular time. I did not participate, and I'm not a historian. I don't want to work it up. I just want to concentrate on specific questions given to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that you took over your duties in 1994, which means after the facts. But before 1994, I think you were at NATO headquarters. Where were you exactly in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir? 1993 -- sir, in 1993, I was at the beginning of the year the commandant of the German Command and General Staff College in Hamburg. And in the second half of the year, I took over the 3rd German Corps in Koblenz, and by doing that I basically prepared the German operations for Somalia, which were then finished in 1994. And very shortly after we had redeployed from Somalia, we got our first mission to prepare ourselves for an UNPROFOR mission in Croatia, in Trojica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for that clarification. My last question before the break: You have also explained at the very beginning of your testimony last Monday that you attended an educational institution in the United States, in Kansas, where you of course met with American officers but also apparently officers from the ex-Warsaw Pact countries. Can you confirm that in Kansas you were in a position to have contacts with officers from the ex-Warsaw Treaty countries?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I may, I might clarify this. I had connections with former -- with JNA officers, Yugoslav officers. One was sitting right behind me. And they were not members of the Warsaw Pact. By that time, the Warsaw Pact was still very efficient. And I had no other members of the Warsaw Pact working with us. We had a lot of officers who had their training before in Moscow, like officers from Afghanistan, from Ethiopia, and in other countries with whom we could compare their experience there, in Russia and the experience in the United States. And a lot of my experience which I got with former Warsaw Pact countries, where once the Wall came down, where I had to take responsibility for the unification of the East German, West German army, and being the commandant of the Command and General Staff College, I was the first NATO general to attend the highest institutions, as far as educational institutions was concerned, in Moscow, in Budapest, in Warsaw, in Prague, so again I had very good installations and rapport with many of those officers from then, but this was in 1990 -- in 1991 following. This was not at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas in 1975-1976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA officer who was sitting behind you with who you certainly conversed, did he give you the impression of having the same kind of training as an officer in a Western army or from a NATO country? Technically speaking, this officer from the JNA, did he appear to you to have had the same kind of training as you yourself? And being with you means that he was attending a specific course, like you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I may, there were two general -- two officers, and they were totally different. One officer was a young captain; this was the one sitting behind me. An infantry officer -- by the way, a Muslim infantry officer from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mehmed Bazic [phoen], a very nice and very intelligent young officer, who basically I had the feeling had similar experience in command and control as I had them in the German army. The other officer was an officer of the Security Services of the former Yugoslav army, Dusan Omerovic, who was just sent there to take care of his younger brother, to -- to take care that this guy behaved appropriately to the Yugoslav way of living. So he was the shadow, and he was a -- a typical security officer I -- which -- and these people are totally different from the normal officers who are fighting the battle. So this was very interesting to see these two people harnessed in the same course. And just to give you an example how difficult it was for them, once this Dusan Omerovic, who was a colonel in the Yugoslav army and had to prevent to be a captain only in -- in Fort Leavenworth, once he came back into Yugoslavia, he committed suicide because he just could not stand the difference of what he had been learned and what he has went through in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. This dichotomy of having been an officer of his country and seeing that the situation was totally different from the one he expected this made him commit suicide. And this was also a very bad experience for me because I thought very highly of this officer, and we had long, long evenings discussing things of our -- of our profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are confirming that, a priori, the training of JNA officers was training, meeting the standards required of a modern army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is 10.30. We're going to have the break, and we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Reinhardt, I'll continue with my questions now according to the following plan: I will ask you questions that are directly linked to your report, which you should have before you. Having asked you some questions that relate to paragraphs that I will mention in your report, I will ask you some general questions, which will still be based on the documents that you have been provided with, questions that will have to do with UNPROFOR, questions that have to do with civilian and military authorities. I will then go back to the subject of the Mujahedin, to the subject of prisoners, and I will also deal with technical and military issues. With regard to your report, you have already answered many questions concerning your report, but I think that certain issues could be better clarified. In paragraph 2.2 of your report, you provided a definition of the mission and responsibility of a superior. In paragraph 2.11, you said that the superior is personally responsible for the conduct of all the operations -- all the military operations in his area of responsibility. When you say, "All military operations," does this term include operations that would also be carried out by the corps, other than the 3rd Corps? And I would like to point out that the 3rd Corps would have a geographical -- territorial competence. If there is another corps which had other territorial competence and it intervened in its territorial's own responsibility, in such a case would these military operations be the responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is a question which I would like to answer in two ways: Once you have elements of another corps which support you in your operations and which will be given to you, subordinated to you for that particular operation, they are under your command and you have full responsibility as far as the operations is concerned. It might not be that you have full disciplinary power over them, because this -- they might be attached to you only for a certain period of time and a certain operation. The other possibility is that if there is a larger part of your area of responsibility in which your adjacent corps will take part of that, you just change the boundaries, that this part of the terrain will be taken away from you and given to your neighbouring commander and then you coordinate with him, which you would normally do if this is a larger operation. These are the two possibilities, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to this term "all military actions," as a military expert, would you say that military actions could concern operations carried out by units that might be described as independent or that might have the appearance of military units, although they are paramilitary units or have all the characteristics of a military unit. So when you say "all military actions," in your opinion does this term include paramilitary units or other types of units that have military characteristics?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is my understanding and this is the way I've been trained, that all the forces in the area I am responsible for in my operations, which operate in my area of operations, for everything which they are doing I'm responsible as the highest commander at the end. That's unity of command. Because otherwise, it's very difficult afterwards to distinguish who is responsible for what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. In your report in footnote number 13, you mentioned Article 87(3) of the Supplementary Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions. This Article provides that the party -- that: "High contracting parties to the conflict shall require any commander who is aware that subordinates or other persons under his control are going to commit or have committed a breach of the conventions." When you say, "Persons under his authority," does this mean that you should consider that these persons could also be the Mujahedin? Because in 2.14, you say the following: "A commander has to investigate and to initiate appropriate actions as soon as he becomes aware of alleged or de facto criminal activities in his area of responsibility." Does this mean that individuals who are active in a command area, would this mean that they come under the Article 87(3) of Supplementary Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions in purely military terms?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this is my understanding that all the forces under -- in the area of responsibility of my control are then -- I'm taking responsibility for what they're doing and I have to do something about this. Not only Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for the forces which are under my direct command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2.17 of your report - and I'm still talking about the same matter - you refer to the rules that concern the application of international humanitarian law by military forces, and you inferred -- you extracted the following phrase from this rule. It's contained in your report, but I will read it out for the sake of the transcript and for the sake of those who are following these proceedings via Internet. This is what you said: "An officer shall be personally liable for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that units subordinate to him or other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violations and if he failed to take measures to prevent such violations at a time when it was still possible to prevent their commission." It seems that given this reference you have made -- the rules in force in ex-Yugoslavia gave certain responsibility to an officer, certain general and overall responsibility over all such units and individuals who may have committed violations. This is what you said in paragraph 2.17. Would you confirm what is stated under paragraph 2.17.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I quoted this because I thought this was a very key paragraph for the basic understanding of the responsibility of a commander, of everything going on in his area of responsibility. Therefore, I quoted it. I think it's a key understanding for the way a commander should react to things even by people who are not under his direct command but acting in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to explain what you said -- what you wrote, yesterday you said that the military situation was very complex, given that there were a number of fronts; there were the Serbs and the Croats; there was the problem of refugees. So, in fact, the situation was extremely complex. No one would dispute this, given the answers that you have provided, the questions you have asked yourself. But in terms of military strategy, what took place at the time and in light of the documents that you were provided with - because you told us that you worked on the basis of these documents alone - the conflicts that occurred and the military actions taken were these large-scale actions or small-scale actions carried out by small units with very precise objectives. For example, taking control of a village where there were about 50 persons, or were these actions large-scale military actions? Did military forces advance, take enemy positions, et cetera? In military terms and on the basis of the documents you examined, how would you assess the military action in the field, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, normally if you talk about corps operations, you talk about large-size operations of heavy and large units. If I might turn to the -- unfortunately, it's the other side of the map, but we realised yesterday that throughout the time the basic front lines have not changed very much, so these were operations in which brigades, sometimes also more than one brigade, were involved but the majority of those actions were rather small-scaled actions, which was also normal because of the professional capabilities. Small-scale actions were capable of being conducted; large-scale actions were much more difficult to coordinate and also to support. So this was not big movement back and forth; this was basically fighting over individual terrain, features, villages, roads of communications. Nevertheless, sir, I must say this was a very busy operation, as far as the corps headquarters was concerned, because it was a variety of skirmishes and operations going on parallel in the entire area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer. I am still talking about operational matters. You came to the conclusion on the basis of the documents that you had that there was the operational group of Bosnian Krajina [as interpreted] that was in existence, and in paragraph 36 of your report you said that this operational group was a tactical centre.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Its objective was to coordinate the operations of various units. Does that mean that this tactical centre was more or less independent of the 3rd Corps Command? Was it free to manoeuvre as it saw fit or to coordinate units? Was this something that could only be done under the control of the 3rd Corps, if it wanted to coordinate the action of units? We should point out that this new BH army was composed of a lot of officers from the former JNA and could function as the former armies from the East functioned. So my question is precise: This operational group, was it able to take liberty when operating, or did it only take action under the authority and command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you remember that we were talking about the span of command yesterday. Taking into consideration that the 3rd Corps operated between 17 and 19 brigades, plus 14 municipal defence councils, this is just a span of command nobody can control. Normally in the military we say maximum is six subordinate units which you can somehow still control. Therefore, it was normal and logic that between the corps and the brigades you had some organisation coordinated on behalf of the corps, subordinate units. In normal -- in other armies, this is normally a division, headquarters doing that. Here it is an operational group, an ad hoc group with a rather small staff which acts on behalf of the corps commander executing the operations and the will of the corps commander.
