So this operational group will not act independently; it will act only on behalf of a mission given by the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now discuss the matter of professionalism within the BH. It's paragraph 5.12 in your report. You said that there were deficiencies in the command structure, that there were losses that they had in the course of combat and that the BH was constantly being reorganised, and you drew the conclusion that there was a low level of professionalism in tactical military terms. So you said that when you take all the elements into consideration, that in tactical and military terms you would say that the level of professionalism was not very high. Would you confirm this opinion of yours and did you make this assessment in relation to the NATO standards? Is this your assessment of the level of professionalism?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The former JNA officers were rather scarce. We have read that only 9 per cent in the headquarters of the 3rd Corps were former officers, and we also read that some of the brigade commanders were no officers at all, had no command and -- and experience as soldiers. So that shows that this was very, very difficult to organise complex operations and that you had to do it very simple on the very low level, on the very tactical level, and also control it from higher headquarters maybe more than you would normally do just in order to make sure that the lower headquarters not experienced as it should normally be could do it differently. So I think the corps command was under very, very adverse situation because the other thing which you just mentioned is that he had to build up more or less from scratch territorial forces which were in the country and additional forces which were being built up during that time, making them operational. And it always takes a time until they become operational, and at the same time fighting an enemy. And therefore, this flexibility and this constant flux that you didn't have solid structures, which we in the military are normally used to, that you have constantly different subordinate and superior factions you had to rely upon made it very difficult, because military operations very much rely on confidence, on loyalty to your subordinates and your superiors, that you know each other, that you know how the other reacts. If you don't know that, because this is this flux of situation, it makes it very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To take control of a location where there are about 10 or maybe 100 inhabitants, in military terms is it necessary to have a very high level of professionalism or is it sufficient to have a small, determined unit in order to do this quite easily, and particularly if they know in advance that the village is being defended by civilians accompanied by some HVO soldiers? In order to take control of a place - X, for example - is it really necessary to have a high level of professionalism, a high level of competence?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, for the soldier on the ground, the army, which is all about his platoon commander, maximum, his company commander, because everything above that is unknown to him. So the professionalism for the soldier is his direct commander who leads him into fire. And everybody who is attacking a village is scared to death whether he is a soldier or not because he doesn't know the results. And nobody wants to go there to become a hero or a martyr afterwards. So if you don't have a professional leadership in which you trust, you probably don't leave your trench. And therefore professionalism in this regard I think is even more important than professionalism on higher headquarters, because that is what the army really makes it all about. And you -- you can see in the documents and some of the papers the 3rd Corps and the 7th Mountain Brigade have prepared that they complain about the poor standards, especially on the infantry level as platoon and company commanders being incompetent, being not capable of doing their job in order to motivate their soldiers to do what they're supposed to do. So the professionalism on this low level is really what an army is all about, not the high brass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Having -- bearing in mind what you said, the superior levels of the command who are aware that operations in the field, because of a lack of training or competence of those involved in the action, and they know that this might result in failings, in gaps, as a result, might the command have to be especially careful in that they are aware of the fact that they don't have what they need, as far as training is concerned?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think they -- they try to do as much as possible of retraining them in the operational pauses and to prepare them for the fight in front of them, which is possible, which has been done, and which had to be done in every army to keep the level as high as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still referring to your report, and then I'll move on to other issues. Paragraph 9.4.10, in that paragraph you mentioned the -- Mr. Siber, the deputy of Halilovic, who having carried out an inspection, reported the existence of criminal activities in the 3rd Corps area, and you said - and this is contained in your report - that Siber proposed that the deputy commander be dismissed; that is to say, that Merdan be dismissed. And you said that Siber's report was thrown into the wastebasket. These are the terms that you yourself used. Within the NATO system, if a similar situation -- if an identical situation had occurred, would it be logical to request that the second-in-command be dismissed, not the first-in-command? Why the second-in-command? Why not the first-in-command? How do you explain that within this system one wanted to punish the second-in-command, not the first-in-command? What military criteria are used when requesting that the deputy be punished and not the first-in-command? How would you as a general explain this? If you had had to deal with such a situation, what position would you have adopted?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. If I may, the trash bin is not my word. I just quoted it from that telephone conversation. But it seems to me, also from other reports which I have read on General Merdan, that some people in the area said that General Merdan has been involved in illegal activities and that they were not very happy with his way of doing business. There are also other reports in the documents that -- from a municipal standpoint people said, "He is not doing his job properly." And I think this is the main reason why Siber said, "If this is the case and if he is replacing you and if he is covering up illegal or criminal activities, he has to go." Now, in the normal way of business in NATO countries, if you have a deputy covering up things and if you are aware of that, if you -- if you yourself are covering him up, then you are to do -- to go and you are due to leave your job. Now, I don't know how much General Hadzihasanovic knew about these allegations, and probably it was the first time that he was confronted himself with this kind of allegations in this telephone call. As long as he takes the appropriate steps to relieve his deputy, because his deputy is not acting according to the law and the military rules, then I think it's all right. If he is covering up, he will be in deep trouble. At least, he would be in deep trouble in my army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document mentioned in paragraph 9.4.10, it was one which was relevant at the period in question. I've checked this. You were provided with a declaration of war. It's P362, but you were provided with this declaration of war, which was signed by President Izetbegovic. Normally a declaration of a state of war gives arise to a legal situation for an army, because we no longer have peacetime; it is a state of war. In a state of war, if Mr. Siber suggests that Halilovic dismisses someone, wouldn't you say that this is the responsibility of the president in office, Mr. Izetbegovic? As a member of the military, how would you assess this issue, if we are dealing with wartime and not peacetime, if we are dealing with something that occurred in wartime?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this report, which -- from which -- this telephone report doesn't show that Mr. Siber actually wrote a report to the President Izetbegovic and he advised him to replace Mr. Merdan, but I don't know about the consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall now address another issue, and that is the question of UNPROFOR on the ground. There are documents that were given to you which indicate that the UN through its representatives - that is, the forces that were deployed there - did play a role. In Exhibit P275, it is a document perhaps you don't have in front of you, but you did have it in your possession, because I checked, and it was signed by several parties to the conflict: General Mladic, General Delic, General Petkovic, two other persons, and General Morillon, who represented UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document speaks of cessation of hostilities among the parties signing the document dated the 15th of June, 1993, at 15.07 hours, and it is also indicated in this document that the parties pledge to respect the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949. In view of the fact who signed this document, wasn't it up to the signatories to make sure that the Geneva Conventions are respected, especially with regard to the question of prisoners, their conditions of detention? And by signing this document, wasn't there a commitment on the part of all the parties, including representatives of UNPROFOR, to make sure that the Geneva Conventions are respected? If you had signed it -- first of all, would you have signed it? And what would you have done, if you had signed it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from discussions with my friend General Morillon how difficult the situation was for him, because he really had no power to execute some of the things he wanted to have executed, and I think Srebrenica is the worst example of that, which then also led to the situation that UNPROFOR was changed into IFOR, where we as the International Community were capable of using the power in our hands, which we were not during UNPROFOR. But nevertheless, I would have signed it if I had been in the position like that, and I would have looked -- I would have looked at the prisoners of war would have been treated the best way possible, and by doing that I would have gone to those prisons or had sent my representative to those prisons to check how the prisoners of war have been treated by that particular time and have taken the appropriate action if they were not treated accordingly. And we know from many pictures that this was not the case, notwithstanding which side took the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document which was tendered and was not contested, and the number of the document is P289, dated the 25th of April, and it is a document of the 3rd Corps regarding the consequences of Miletici, and it is stated in this document -- no, I'm sorry, it doesn't come from the 3rd Corps but from the Croatian side, because it was drawn up by the Vitez Brigade. Therefore, this document has to do with the Miletici case, because the brigade in question received a telephone call from one of the persons who was on the spot. And it is indicated in this document that in the afternoon representatives of UNPROFOR visited the persons that had been arrested. How can one explain that knowing that people had been arrested under illegal conditions and when one represents an army belonging to NATO, should one act and call on the parties responsible, remind them of their rights? Shouldn't they be told, "You have no right to keep these people in detention," because there is a specific reference to the Geneva Conventions in the document that has been signed? You told us that you would have visited those detention places, and visiting places where civilians were being held, what would you have done once you saw for yourself the conditions they were in? And wouldn't you have demanded of those holding them to release them?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, please allow to come back to the basic conditions of UNPROFOR, which were very unhappy and unfavourable conditions, because UNPROFOR by that time were allowed to use their power only in self-defence and, on the other hand, to monitor. They were not allowed - and I think this was the big mistake in UNPROFOR - to take active actions on their own. What you said is absolutely right. I think if you see civilians being taken hostage or prisoners, it would have been necessary to take every action possible to relieve them -- to release them. But all I think the commander of this UNPROFOR unit by that time was able to, to tell the other side to do that, but he was not capable by that time to force the other side to do that. He was deliberately dependent on the goodwill of the other side. And we both know that at the end this was just very insufficient and therefore the UNPROFOR regime did not -- did not do the job they were supposed to do at the very beginning. And I only can tell you that this is a very, very adverse situation. If you know that something doesn't go according to your ideas and your provisions given to you, but you are not able to execute this because the regime under which you work - and this regime, the United Nations regime of UNPROFOR - did not allow you to do more. So I absolutely agree with you there should have been done more, but politically by that period of time it seems not to have been possible to do more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall now move on to another subject, and that is the mixture between the military and civilian authorities. You referred several times in your answers to this and I shall rely exclusively on the documents that you had. I was referring a moment ago to the declaration of the state of war, which was issued on the 20th of June, 1992 and which led to the mobilisation for the defence of the territory and calling on all citizens between 18 and 65 to respond, men and women, and it is indicated in paragraph 3 of this decision that these will be forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina which are authorised to take all necessary measures to organise the resistance of the people in order to put an end to the existing situation obviously. Therefore, this document attaches a very important role to the army. And one could have the impression that the civilian authority at that point in time could have become dependent upon the military authorities. What is your own impression looking through the documents? And did you ask yourself the question as to the freedom that the military command had - specifically the 3rd Corps - with respect to the civilian authorities? What could you tell us and what additional explanations could you provide the Chamber with in that regard?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quite sure whether my answer will be a correct one. This is just a best guess. The way I see it, the civil organisations within the area of responsibility of a corps still existed, and there were independent organisations. But the corps commander was due to cooperate with them to the utmost in order to synergise all the forces and all the elements in his area of responsibility for the sake of the defence of this area. I don't think that he had command over these civil authorities, but the way of persuasion of discussion of negotiation in a way to support his military activities were very obvious, and he did this, and I think the majority -- not the majority. I think all the organisations in that area were eager to support him in his -- in his intentions to defend the country. But I don't believe that one could say he was the military governor or dictator in that area, everything under his control. I think there was a lot of -- of negotiation and persuasion and discussion between the institutions. And I think these civil organisations remained independent through the operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could you explain -- if you see a document. There's a document admitted into evidence. The number is 00809149, coming from the War Presidency of Zenica; that is, the Municipality of Zenica, the War Presidency of Zenica, which is the place where the 3rd Corps was situated. And I'm reading you Article 1 of this document: "The commands in question must immediately order unconditional cease-fire. All units must return to barracks." And this order, issued by the War Presidency, was sent to the 3rd Corps of the army, and I have evidence of that. How would you explain this?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a -- a municipal defence council in a variety of cities. I think there were 14 in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. And they commanded troops, and they commanded troops under the command of the 3rd Corps. And I think if this war council, which is probably running this municipal defence staff, wants to cease actions, to cease actions at that particular time, he was due to give an order like this. Now, I don't think this was an order to the 3rd Corps. I think this was probably making sure that the 3rd Corps knows about the orders. I think this was -- but I don't have that paper in front of me. This was at least not an order which a war council could give to the 3rd Corps to make the 3rd Corps happen in a certain way. This was only for their forces under the war council's command and control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still on this issue, there is a document with the number P204, issued by the 3rd Corps and which has to do with the military police of the 306th Brigade. And this military order says that the MUP, which means the civilian police, and the military police and other brigades are resubordinated to the 306th Brigade. How is it that a military document can place under military authority a police which is basically civilian, which is the MUP, depending on the Ministry of the Interior, unless the military authority has extensive powers over the civilian authorities? What do you think as an expert witness about this particular situation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, whenever I hear the term "MUP," my hair grows up, raises up, because most of the atrocity which I have seen in Kosovo were committed not by the military but by the MUP. It's a paramilitary organisation which created most of the atrocities I have seen, and it's a part -- they are in uniform. They are also working with military equipment. They have tanks. They have armoured personnel carrier, and they fought side by side with the military. And I think they did the same thing on the other side in -- in that particular case you're talking about. And therefore, it's a blurred situation. I don't know, and I must tell you I just don't know whether the corps was authorised to take them under their command. At least, I think, there must have been a clear understanding between the military -- between the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior that these forces would synergise their efforts on the ground in order to fight together side by side. I think for you and for a layman there is no way to differentiate between the military and the MUP by the way they operated on the ground. And this is a thing which we are totally unfamiliar with in our armies, but I think we just have to see this special status of the MUP, and I assume based on the documents I have read that the conditions of the -- of the MUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as the war capabilities, the fighting capabilities were concerned, were similar to the ones which I have encountered after I came to Kosovo between the Serb MUP and the Serb armed forces. For me there was no way to differentiate what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A final question regarding this question of military and civilian authorities: There is a document, P272, dated the 28th of July, 1993, and it is the code for the units of the 3rd Corps and each unit has a number, a reference number. And reading this document, I note that the civilian authority, the municipal authority also has a number, and we find that the municipal authority had four anti-sabotage detachments with a number given to each, and they appear in this military document. What do you think of that? Have you seen that document? And in your opinion, what would this anti-sabotage unit be?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: These anti-sabotage units were units for irregular warfare, like -- very similar to the guerilla. And we also saw that there were guerilla warfare -- guerilla groups in some of the municipality defence staffs. And, sir, if you remember yesterday, we got this organisational chart by the Defence in which we saw the individual brigades commanded by the 3rd Corps, and 14 - I think I remember from my work - 14 different municipal defence councils which were military territorial organisations. We remember that the 3rd Corps was based on the former territorial organisation which had military forces responsible for the defence of their area, of their villages, and in this regard these military -- these territorial forces were put under the command of the corps, therefore they had those numbers, and therefore they had forces, including these sabotage forces, which are forces not familiar to us in NATO, but they were doing irregular operations in the -- in the area of operations of that municipality council, defence council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Still referring to this same document which refers to the numbers of units, their equipment and weapons, which tells us how the 3rd Corps was in fact armed. And under the number 018, there's a indication "sniper rifle." Was it customary for competent armies, qualified -- proper armies to have sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And it still is. And we have in all our armies sniper rifles, and we have soldiers specially trained as becoming snipers. And we all might remember that the territorial organisation was very much based on a partisan kind of warfare for the defence if Yugoslav should be attacked and occupied. And for this kind of partisan movement, snipers are very important, and also anti-sabotage troops are important to fight an unconventional guerilla kind of warfare against an enemy. And therefore, they were a logical part, from their point of view, within their territorial army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall move on to another topic, which has already been broadly covered by questions of Judges, and that is the position of prisoners. You responded to all the questions, but I just have some minor details to discuss with you. There is a document that you have had, P260, which is a document written by the security sector of the 3rd Corps and addressed to all brigade commanders and which has to do with the way in which they should behave in the case of prisoner exchanges and the measures that need to be taken. It appears in this document that when there is a prisoner exchange the released prisoner is debriefed and he has to answer a whole series of questions according to a text, which is quite lengthy and consists of several pages, and he is asked where he was captured, the hour, the time, the place of his capture, was he armed, was he imprisoned, his name, et cetera, et cetera. And therefore there's a number of questions that have to be put to the prisoner. This document addressed to the brigades should normally affect ABiH prisoners detained by the HVO and who are debriefed. To the extent to which you saw this document - I assume you did - when the ABiH detained HVO prisoners, shouldn't they have also asked them just their name, the unit they belonged to, and shouldn't the questioning be limited to this: According to the training that you had and the training provided in all armies of the world, the questioning of prisoners, how far can it go?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have the document with me right now, but I remember the document, and I -- I cannot find the numbers the way -- the PT numbers, because I have them listed in another category; therefore, I'm sorry, I don't find it so fast. But basically the question is that if you become a prisoner you are allowed to tell your name, your rank, and your serial number, and that's it. You even are not allowed, based on the international regulations, which unit you are coming from. So this also applied to the HVO officers -- HVO prisoners of war coming into your area. In addition to that, we -- we know that almost all armies do it differently, trying to get more out of the enemy, as far as information is concerned. Now, once your own soldiers, having been held prisoner on the other side, come back - in this case, ABiH soldiers coming back, having been released as prisoners of war from the HVO - I think it's normal procedure that you would ask them the maximum, where they have been, how they have been treated, what they have been up to, in order to get the intelligence and also to make sure they have been treated appropriately. I think this is not against the basic humanitarian law, because once they are back, they are soldiers under your command again and then they have to answer all the questions pertinent to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a specific case. In a military operation, you capture prisoners, so you have enemy prisoners. In concrete terms, what instructions would you give your troops with regard to those prisoners? What is the minimum threshold and the maximum one with respect to those prisoners? What instructions would you yourself give regarding the management of these people who have been made prisoner?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there's a clear legal obligation, and the legal obligation is that you are not allowed to ask more than the three items I mentioned before. And if you do that, you always already commit an illegal act concerning the international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a military operation, when you capture prisoners, if there are prisoners who appear to be civilians, should they be taken to a military prison when they are civilians and possibly even minors? How would a modern army, which respects democratic criteria, treat civilians, women, old people, and children that are taken captive, according to NATO countries' rules and the rules of the ex-Soviet bloc?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if you occupy an area and you have civilian population there, it can be evacuated. It has to be treated and supported. But they cannot become prisoners, because they're civilians. Once they are treated and have medical support and -- and logistic support, you have to make sure that they are being transported in an area in which they are not affected any more by the adverse conditions of a war. So you cannot put them in the same conditions as prisoners of war. If you do this, you basically jeopardise their well-being and you are against the law, no matter -- no matter what country you're belonging to, because the international law applies to all the nations who have -- have subscribed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're telling us applies virtually to all the armies of the world; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going on now to address the question of Mujahedin. You answered a series of questions about this. You mentioned the Mujahedin in your report. But I should like to address this issue solely in military terms. The situation at the time, such as it appeared to be on the basis of the documents and your report, there was the 3rd Corps, which had a geographic area under its control and it constituted -- it consisted of about 32.000 troops under its control, deployed on the ground under difficult conditions. That is without doubt. However, in military terms, could one envisage a unit of some 100 individuals being able to impose a reign of terror; whereas, an army corps, which is fully equipped, has mortars and everything else, cannot put an end to the activities of this so-called independent unit waging war in its own way? Is this feasible, in military terms? Is it a possibility?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, sir. As a military commander, I have the means and I have the power to check what these people were doing, and if I am not agreeing with what they're doing, if I disagree with their way of waging war, I have the means to stop them from doing that. That might not be a very easy way, but I have possibility to do that and I should have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the documents you were provided with, documents concerning the 3rd Corps units, et cetera, on the basis of the material you were provided with, did the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 3rd Corps have the military means to disarm, to annihilate a unit composed of about 100 individuals?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they had it. And if I may -- might draw your attention back to the basic order for the -- in which -- before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to address that.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because yesterday a document was mentioned, a document which said that -- in a report that mentioned various solutions, either to integrate them, or to refuse them hospitality, or to disarm them. You must be referring to this document that the Trial Chamber is perfectly familiar with, because we've been working on this case for over eight months now. The document that you are familiar with - and I'm speaking purely in military terms - was it an order of some sort, an implicit or explicit order to the 3rd Corps commander, ordering him to take action, an order to take action against this unit which wasn't respecting the legitimate authority of those who were in control of the 3rd Corps's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me this was a clear order. Thank you, sir, for helping me. And I think it also showed that there was a way, an alternative to do something about it, rather than leaving it as -- as it was by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the documents that you have been provided with - I'm referring to P294, in particular, a document from the 3rd Corps, and I'm referring to the intelligence sector of the 3rd Corps and the part that concerns mercenaries - this document requests that their names be provided, the location of the unit that they are in, and it requests other details, et cetera. On the basis of the documents you had, independently of the Mujahedin, who may have come not to act as mercenaries or maybe for other reasons, were there any foreigners or even local people who had the status of mercenaries? Because if this document mentions them, it means that there was a problem, as far as mercenaries are concerned.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it's not that I'm aware of that there were other mercenaries in that area of the 3rd Corps. There certainly were civilians who had weapons, as former trained soldiers in the JNA or in the territorial forces who could not join the military in time and who were defending their villages with the weapons available to them. But I think these people could not be called mercenaries. These were just people trying to defend their house or the house of their neighbour and their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to move on to the last subject so as not to use up time unnecessarily, and I want to discuss purely technical and military matters. In the situation at the time, and bearing in mind the difficulties of the 3rd -- that the 3rd Corps had to encounter, the problem of the competence of the officers, given the geographical problems, the problems of communication and transport, when an attack was organised, in your opinion, and on the basis of the documents you were provided with, should there have been before military action was taken a preparatory phase for this action? Is it customary before launching a military action to have a meeting to decide what one is going to do and how one is going to act, in order to determine the objectives of the action? Usually, and on the basis of the documents you were provided with, is this how one proceeded?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I just take the level of a brigade or a battalion. You take your commanders, you get your commanders together before you attack. You give them your order. You basically discuss with them your concept of operations. And on a lower level, very often, at least in my army, we then war gamed this on a relief like this, or what we call a sandbox, in which we try to run through the entire operation and tell on -- on the sandbox or on the relief what unit was supposed to do what, because it's normally a very complex situation and the biggest -- the biggest thing you want to -- to prevent is that people shoot themselves, fratricide. So everybody has to know who is where, at what time you have to coordinate this, and coordination really means to go through step by step with the individuals who are commanding these operations. And I think, from the documents I have read, that this procedure was more or less the same in the JNA and also in the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the documents that you have examined, when the BH launched an attack, would you say that the units in the field, perhaps at the level of a section or a platoon, at the level of a small unit, would you say that in view of all the difficulties caused by the geographical situation -- should these units have had permanent radio contact with either the operational group, which was the tactical centre, or with the headquarters? Could you imagine action being taken outside of the control of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, sir, the communication which you have is with your next level; i.e., the platoon commander with the company commander, except if it's a special platoon, which then can talk also to the battalion commander; the battalion, normally with the brigade; and the brigade with the operational group or directly with the corps command; and the corps operational centre, which has been established, as we have seen from many documents. But normally the corps would not know all the details of the ongoing battle down of the company and battalion level except that this was very special, where the commander would say, "I want to know exactly what was going on." You normally don't fight the battle of the lower level because you have, hopefully, a competent commander in whom you trust that he can do that. So the information of what has happened then flows into your headquarters by message forms, be it written messages, be it oral messages from lower headquarters, but already screened by the operational group or by the battalion or the brigade, depending what level has been intermixed between the corps level and the executive level, which is normally the company on the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that theoretically those at the lower level have to report to those above them and at each stage they report on the advancement of the operations to the authority immediately above them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's take an example: The unit in a field takes 10 or 15 prisoners, for example. The unit that takes these prisoners, will it report to the authority above them that they have arrested these individuals or that individuals have surrendered? Will this then go right up the chain of command? Will this information go right up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no, sir. We have seen in Dusina that the company who has taken prisoners has reported this, and this went up the command immediately, because this was the first outbreak of war. I think after two or three months of a war, if a company would take 10 prisoners, that would probably not go up to the highest headquarters; therefore, I say it really depends very much so. It would be up to the battalion commander and the brigade commander -- actually, to -- to analyse the situation whether he would report this to higher headquarters or whether he would include this in his normal combat report, which is due during combat every six hours anyhow, and then that would be a part in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in such a report, should one immediately inform the authority above one the number of wounded, the number of killed, the number of people killed on the other side? According to the military rules, is it necessary to have an almost immediate report on the situation after the last shot has been fired?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there is a constant message flow going to higher headquarters, and in that message flow the question about the enemy and the situation of the enemy and prisoners and casualties is what we say SOP, standard operation procedures, which you crank in. And as I said, every six hours in the Bosnian army the commander was supposed to give a message about the situation on the ground. And I think the same as it is in our army, this would also be a part in their army to do that. Now, if you have a very large number which you had not foreseen, there might be a spot report which you give immediately high up. You say, "Okay, we have 100 or 150 prisoners of war, a very high number of casualties on the other side," which never happened during that particular war. But again, you know, it's up to the commander how he sees the situation, what he then brings up forward immediately or through his routine report, and every six hours is a routine report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we take the example of an enemy who had men who were killed. When the company in the field returns, is there a debriefing stage, and the higher level authority that wasn't present asks those who were fighting in the field about the conditions in which the enemy was killed, et cetera? This stage that follows the action, is this a phase about which a report is made and it is then forwarded to the headquarters? This report is then forwarded to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. After an action is over, you have a debriefing in your own unit and you discuss the problems you ran into, about the good things and also very often the bad things which you have done. I mean, which did not -- which was not successful. And then the commander will write an after-action report. And we have quite a few after-action reports in the documents given to me in which a battalion or a company or a brigade would basically go through the disposition of the operations, the execution, and the problems they run into. And normally under conditions like this, they also would treat the situation of the enemy and about possible casualties on the other side and prisoners of war. And these after-action reports are normally - and I saw this also in the Bosnian army - due very immediately after the action has ceased, in order to inform higher headquarters how it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 330, the 22nd of December, 1992, which is a report from the 3rd Corps and concerns the situation of various brigades under the command of the 3rd Corps. I'm referring to this document, and I will read from it. It's been provided to you. With regard to the 17th Brigade -- not the 7th; the 17th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It mentions the structure of the troops, and the term in English is "the poor" and "criminals." On criminals." Does this mean that in the 17th Brigade soldiers who were delinquent had been incorporated or soldiers who were very poor? Do you recall having read this document? It's dated the 22nd of December, 1992, just before the 1993 period, and it mentions the state of each brigade or company. With regard to the 17th Muslim Brigade, the following is said: "This brigade had special recruitment circumstances. The brigade was up to 75 per cent of full strength. The communications system was not sufficient. Morale was good. As far as the transport of troops is concerned, soldiers still had problems." Do you recall having seen this document? Because this document says that the 17th Brigade and the 7th Brigade are those most capable of conducting offensive operations. Does this remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I remind the document. Having read the document, I don't have it with me right now. But I myself asked a question on those criminals, and I don't know whether they had delinquents or former criminals in their units or not. I only know that the 7th Brigade and in particular the 7th Mountain Brigade was seen as very capable and -- and very thrusting organisation, military units in the 3rd Corps sector, and I remember that there are reports of the 3rd Corps stating that the commanding general would be happy to have other forces being as capable as the 7th Mountain Brigade. But again, the particular question you asked me on those criminals, I -- I'm not capable of answering that to you. I didn't follow it up any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the documents you were provided with, which were very different, there are lists of arms too. On the basis your assessment of the BH and the HVO, who in your opinion seemed to be the best equipped in military terms? Who do you express an opinion about, the state of the forces present in the field? In particular, in the 3rd Corps's zone of responsibility. In military terms, what your -- would your assessment be of the balance of forces involved?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, sir, the best forces, as far as the organisation and the equipment was concerned were the forces of the Republika Srpska. And that's obvious because they were former JNA forces which were just turned into forces of the Republika Srpska. So these were organised forces based on the same doctrine. They had all the equipment with them in country, and they were organised and equipped to the state of the art of equipment by that time in the Yugoslav army. The Croatian forces basically had to build up, but there has been a Croatian state before the Bosnia and Herzegovina state -- Bosnia-Herzegovina existed. They were supported very much also by the Americans at the beginning in the training and also to some way in providing them weapons. And I think the ones who had the poorest training and the poorest equipment were the Bosnian forces, because they had nothing to rely upon. They could take the weapons which were stored in the territorial forces, which were basically spreading all over the former Yugoslavia geography. They could use those. They could use the weapons which they basically took from the other side. They also -- and that becomes rather obvious -- got money from Arab countries to buy weapons on the free market, which I think was one of the reasons Izetbegovic was rather lenient towards the mercenaries, the Mujahedin in the area, because this was quid pro quo that he got the money from them. But I think the most difficult part of the three armies was on the side of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it basically had to start with almost nothing and try to incorporate all these elements which they got from different sides into one reliable and -- and workable organisation, and this was very difficult. So heavy equipment, like heavy artillery, like tanks, like armoured personnel carriers, like helicopters were almost non-existent. There were some tanks but only in very scarce areas. And he hadn't had a chance, the commanding general, to fight a combined-arms army, as we will call this in NATO terms, where you have all these elements of the air, of far-reaching artillery, of - excuse me - of helicopters fighting against one objective. This was just not possible. He just had to take what he was available for. And the majority were infantry weapons, rifles, machine-guns, hand grenades, and mortars. And mortars are not a very far-reaching weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the documents that you have examined did you find proof that the BH had supply routes from abroad? Because you said that in your opinion that must have been the case. Are you absolutely sure of this? And where could they have obtained these supplies from, since it seems that there were lots of HVO checkpoints on the routes, there was a Serb presence too. How could weapons have arrived from the outside, given that the situation on the ground could have made it difficult for such weapons to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I had five battalions day and night in Kosovo guarding the borders towards the surrounding terrain, also very difficult mountainous terrain. And I think we were very competent in trying to prevent weapons to be smuggled in. We were not very successful. To smuggle weapons in an area is a rather easy thing, with cars driving around, with a very broken terrain where you can take mules or -- or personal carriers getting this in. So this was not very difficult. And weapons are to be bought all over the world because there are many weapons dealers who are happy to sell their weapons whoever gets the money from -- for. So to get weapons in the country, even if you just air drop them into the zone, is possible, but you have to have money. And there are some documents which I went through where it says, "Do we have or do we have to be nice to the Mujahedin because they are providing us weapons or their countries are providing money with which we can buy weapons?" So I only deduct from those documents that there must have been some relation, and we know that -- how difficult it was at the beginning for the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina to have support from the outside, and they needed support from the outside because they hadn't had -- they haven't had anything by that time. So without the support from the outside, they couldn't increase their -- their amount of weapons, and it's not only weapons. What is even more important is ammunition. And ammunition normally is very heavy, it's very expensive, and it has to fit your weapons systems. But again, to get this into a country, it seems that the imagination and intuition of the ones who do that is much high higher than we normally would anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I don't think the Judges have any other questions for you. It's time for the break now. The Prosecution will ask questions last. How much time does the Defence think that they will need for additional questions after the break? Because if you have no other questions, we could perhaps release the witness. But that depends on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence will have as many questions as the Trial Chamber, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The best solution would be to have the break now. It's half past 12.00. We'll resume at 1.00. Mr. Mundis, how much time will you need for your re-examination? We need to organise our time, because we only have 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you for the opportunity. As of right now, the Prosecution has three questions for the witness following directly from questions put to him by Your Honours. We do believe that we should be permitted to be the final person or final party to put questions to the witness. I -- it's very difficult to predict what additional questions might arise from the Defence, but as of right now, I would think I need five to ten minutes at the most, depending, again, on issues that might arise during the re-cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon, we have heard the Prosecution say that they would need five or ten minutes. 35 or 40 minutes, would that be sufficient for you? In any event, it should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at most we would need five minutes, but it might not be that we even need that amount of time. But if we could be reserved five minutes, that would be appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In theory, we'll follow this plan -- we'll follow our plan, and we will adjourn at 1.45. So we will resume at five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Bourgon, I give you the floor for your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before beginning with my few additional questions, I would like once again to address my apologies to my colleagues in the interpretation booth. They were rather angry yesterday, saying that I spoke too fast, which made their work unbearable. I apologise, and I will do everything I can to reduce the speed of my speech, and I wish to say that we in the Defence have a lot of appreciation for the people who are assisting us in these proceedings, and I will try to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, it is difficult for me at this point in time to exactly know where to begin after four days and so many good questions that have been put to you. Maybe I can just begin by asking you if you can confirm that fighting on two fronts is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very difficult. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, when the two fronts you are facing, even though they have different identities, different roles, nevertheless if both of these fronts you are facing have the same objective, which is to defeat you, it is a difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It definitely is. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where, General, these two fronts you are facing - in this case, the HVO and the VRS - they both have territorial ambitions, and that is to take away your land and to make you disappear.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The level of stress which is created by such a situation will affect everyone at every level, from the president, down to the soldier at the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I totally agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we say that both of these enemies that you are facing, the HVO and the VRS, are both supported materielly, from a logistic point of view, but also from a political point of view by two big states, such as Croatia, on the side of the HVO, and now -- under the new name Serbia, on the side of the VRS, that this even makes things even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at the geographical situation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you fully understand that they had no access to the sea and that they were surrounded by these two states; namely, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the -- and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they even had two different areas of operation; i.e., Central Bosnia and the Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in these circumstances, you will confirm probably once again that the mission of General Hadzihasanovic, what he was asked to do would be in the following order: One, to ensure that the line against the Serbs would not move.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two, to create the 3rd Corps; and three, to try and create the necessary conditions to liberate Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would that be a fair statement of what his mission was?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would also agree that this mission not only would have but that it should have been the main concern of the commanding general.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It definitely was his main concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to divide my supplementary questions in four distinct areas, the first one being the tempo of operations. And I must admit, General, I have a bit of difficulty in following some of your answers today. Would you agree together in the previous days I gave you many circumstances which could impact on the exercise of command by General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your assessment and your answer today, you mentioned that the tempo of operations was somewhat relaxed at times? Did you say that, or is that your -- your words or your assessment?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there were operational pauses. There was not constant fighting throughout the time day and night. There were operational pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you've also said that the lines did not change very much during this time, the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, in comparison to other operations on the corps-level size operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But I did show you, General, the example of Gorazde, where the complete land was taken and Gorazde was completely isolated. Did I show you this example?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this example is not one that is in the 3rd Corps area, so it's not really one that should concern General Hadzihasanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it -- it will have concerned him very much so, because it's a key part of the country he was defending with the 3rd Corps. But I mean, the movement of operations, back and forward, as you would normally have in -- in corps operation is very much reduced in this kind of operations as we see it in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we say, "Normal operations," are we talking normal operations in the books or normal operations in real life?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the books. I talk about the operations as I have analysed them in -- in history. And as we see it, also as of today when we see operations going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I did show you yesterday, General, the example of Zepce and the pocket that was created up in the north and that it was clear from the series of events that the object was to cut off completely the north to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would agree that this is not only an operational objective but that it is in fact a strategic objective not to lose the north.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I also stated yesterday how important it was for General Hadzihasanovic to keep those two shoulders at any cost in order to prevent the breakthrough at that particular part of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And because if he lost those two soldiers, for example -- those two shoulders, sorry, around Vares, that this would have been critical not only for the 3rd Corps but for the state itself.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a disaster for the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that down in the south there was a similar situation with the two shoulders closing in, which would have completely cut the 3rd Corps away from any route leading to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that as far as the HVO is concerned, we also could see from the diagram - correct me if I'm wrong - but that in January these -- the fighting between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was at its beginning?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But that by the time we reached the period from, I would say, May to September there were ongoing front lines inside the area of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's what I called inverted lines, when they had to fight in different directions, even within the 3rd Corps sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the last map we saw yesterday, which was the end of August, then you could see that by that time the area of operation of the 3rd Corps was encircled by three different corps of Serb forces. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you also agree that the area was also occupied in the inside by two operative zones of the HVO army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what forces were operating in -- within the inside, but I assume that what you tell me is appropriate, so yes, sir. But I have never checked on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, both on the documents that you have read and your reading of the situation, that the flow of refugees would have been non-stop throughout the -- throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we discussed the issue of the lack of weapons, and you knew that there was an embargo in place preventing people from getting weapons.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you said that people are very -- have good ideas on how to get and how to smuggle weapons.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But that would apply, for example, in your case in Kosovo, when you have -- when you can smuggle a weapon from the neighbouring country, that would make it possible, even though it's illegal and even though your forces were guarding that border.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not only did they have to face the forces but they also have to go through a neighbouring country before they can get access to the next one. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this would not make it, unless it was an air drop, but there was a no-fly zone, this would have been absolutely impossible for Bosnia to get weapons from the outside.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say absolutely impossible because otherwise -- there were weapons available, and the corps was armed and other corps were armed, not the appropriate way. But if they -- if it had been totally impossible, even this would have probably not been possible. So somewhere weapons came into the area, and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And now, if I mention to you on the tempo of operations, General, some of the things that took place or some of the attacks that were led not by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina but attacks against which they had to defend?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I simply refer here to a number of towns which were part of the indictment laid against General Blaskic. Blaskic, of course, the commander of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew, for example, that in Gornji Vakuf the fighting was there throughout the year non-stop. Did you know that from the documents that you had?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in Busovaca, there was fighting both in January and later throughout the year on at least three different occasions.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also know that. But we also both know that these fightings on those villages or cities were of limited forces amounted -- or being bogged down in those fightings. These were smaller fightings, not large-scale fightings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I mention to you the fighting in Ahmici in April --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- which was probably the single-most or biggest massacre which took place, according to the evidence filed in other cases, was a very big operation.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Carefully planned and carefully executed. And then if I speak to you of the attacks in Travnik, which started as early as April and went out until the summer, would you agree with me that this is ongoing fighting, even if it's not of a high level?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I speak to you of the towns of Nadioci, Pirici, Santici, Stari Vitez, Rotilj, Kiseljak, Loncari, Grbavica, Svinjarevo, Gomionica, Gromiljak, the complete Bila Valley, including Guca Gora, Maljine, and all the sectors in Bugojno, would you agree that all these towns were the object of armed conflict between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- during that period.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, sir. I must say I cannot agree to everything, because I just don't know this and I was sworn in to tell the truth. But I think there were many, many villages which were constantly encountered by either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you understand that there were more than 300 kilometres of front line between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you understand that to maintain the front line there is every day when you maintain a front line some shooting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the use of sniper is a regular -- a regular happening on front lines.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that front line, even though it is not actual fighting on the offensive, you need to place forces there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you need to find the weapons and the ammunition for these forces.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you saw the reports from General Hadzihasanovic even saying that some forces were on the defensive on the lines were actually using more ammunition than other forces who were on the offensive.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very often the case like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General Hadzihasanovic was wondering whether this was a consequence of the troops being less trained or whether this was a consequence of really, because there was lots of activity on the front line.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It could be both.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, during that time, General, the -- you would agree with me -- you will agree with me that during that time, in order to fulfil his mission, General Hadzihasanovic had to create the army, to train his people, to recruit people, to find the necessary resources, to support operations in other corps, and to keep his main supply routes open.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we've heard from the Judges, you were asked -- you were asked questions concerning -- we all understand, and no one is disputing that this was a tough situation. My question to you is: Is all of this in one year, how tough was it? And should we just say, "Well, it's tough but," or would we say, "It was really tough," and we have to take it into consideration?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I never doubted that this was really tough, and I always said it was really tough, and it was very, very difficult to accomplish the mission as the operational commander of the 3rd Corps. I never doubted this a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because you understand, General, you are -- you are the only soldier in this room. You are the only one today who can ensure that this trial will take into consideration the difficulty and the complexity and the almost nightmare through which General Hadzihasanovic had to accomplish his duty. Can you elaborate on this, please.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the deployment of my forces and my personal engagement in Bosnia-Herzegovina was to help those forces who were attacked from the Serbs and the HVO. This was all about why we deployed there. And I have nothing, just high esteem about the way this new government tried to survive with its forces. And if you have the impression that I am in any way against them, then I must tell you this is absolutely wrong. I am absolutely unbiased in this way, rather than being pro-Bosnia-Herzegovina, because this is why I went there. So I see the difficulties. I always stressed the difficulties. And I'm absolutely sure that the Chamber Trial will take this into their considerations, because this is the key factor you have to take into considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I would never even think that you were biassed. My question was more simply related to what I said at the beginning. We are of the view that we need the input of soldiers who can really explain what it could have been like.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned yesterday, General, that when you are shot at, that this significantly reduces automatically your -- I'm not sure what word you used --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your capabilities. Now, you understand from the documents that Zenica was being shelled with artillery throughout the year, not constant fire but regular fire by artillery in the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the town that had grown and had more than doubled in population.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the refugees, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In a town that was starving.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd just like to show you one quick map which refers to one operation, which was lead by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I only have one of them in colour, and I would like you to use the one that is in colour, this one here. Now, General, this is a drawing of the attack on Vares or the operations leading to the capture of Vares. You can see from this map, General, that there are three corps involved in this operation: 1 Corps, 2 Corps, and 3 Corps. And you can also see by looking at the bottom of this map, you see the involvement of the Operational Group Istok.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you know from reading your documents that the Operational Group Istok was then -- was then under command of the newly formed 6 Corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So looking at the geography and bearing in mind that this is a four-corps operation and the way it was handled, would you agree with me at first that this is fighting at the operational level which requires very sophisticated command and control planning and execution?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that, but let me tell you it's not a four-corps operation; it's a three-corps operation, because the Operational Group Istok by that period of time was given to the 1st Corps, attached within the 1st Corps sector. So they were elements of another corps, given to another corps to support them. But nevertheless it was a complicated operation. And it was exactly what I tried to describe in my statement, that over the time the corps became more and more proficient and learnt more and more to execute more complicated operations, because they had to learn it by doing. And this is a good example, a very good example which you pointed forward, that shows that the Bosnian forces have regained -- not regained, but have gained the competencies to do operations like this, as far as the -- the professional capabilities, as far as the weapons, as far as communications was concerned. So they have improved over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And given, General, the starting point of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially the 3rd Corps, if they succeeded in achieving that kind of level of sophistication in mounting an attack or an operation in early November, would you say that this can be attributed to the leadership of the 3rd Corps and to the good work, both the sound military work, training, planning, and preparing of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is to be attributed to the corps commanders of all the corps involved, including General Hadzihasanovic. No question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on, General, to another topic, and that of - quickly, because I don't want to run out of time - but first I'd like to confirm that it is your understanding that the situation you were in in Kosovo was different from the situation in Bosnia, both in respect of your responsibilities that you had, the role that you had, and the applicable law in Kosovo. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not to be compared. Total different scenarios and background.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you make any comments about the MUP in Kosovo, this has -- could have nothing to do with the MUP in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the main document which describes the relationship of the civil authorities with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is the decree having force of law on defence, was never shown to you. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So today you are not able to comment on whether what was still in force or what was not in force at the time these events took place.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am capable of discussing the situation of the military district command in this regard, because they were part of the 3rd Corps. And by the other things, I said I only can assume that this was the way they cooperated. I don't know, and I made very clear that I don't know it exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you saw from documents that there was indeed the civil authorities still operating.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying, General, that your position is that if you are the governor or the military governor of an area, then you would be responsible for anything in that territory? Those are your words today.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is what goes with the term "military governor," that you're responsible for everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is your understanding that this was not the case of General Hadzihasanovic in his area.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in any event, whatever you may have said today, in terms of responsibility, you would agree with me that the only thing that really counts is what law was applicable.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if we find out later or by whatever means that the law applicable was different from your answers, then you understand that -- that this is what is the matter.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You only can apply which -- the law which was applicable at the particular time. And I was asked this morning how I would see it from my point of view, and there might be a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General Hadzihasanovic, as you mentioned, was not responsible for civilians or for the law enforcement of common-law crimes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the area of General Hadzihasanovic, we already confirmed that whether there were members from BritBat, from HVO, from the ECMM, from the ICRC, and from the Army of the Republika Srpska, that he was not responsible for these people or for violations committed by these people.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you are in Bosnia at that time, would you agree with me that you have a governmental army which can be referred to as governmental forces?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you have two other forces; namely, the HVO and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you have a number of internationals which have various legal status.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that everyone else are civilians.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the civilian police was responsible to take care of those other people.
