utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the Mujahedin were not incorporated - we're not talking cooperation - if they were not incorporated in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then their legal status was that of civilians who might have been bearing arms and who were common-law criminals. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were irregulars and not just simple civilians, and I think it's too easy to say a black and white -- black or white, yes or no, because even so they might not have been in the -- incorporated in the overall organisation, they worked very closely within them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And therefore, they're different from normal civilians working or doing things in the area. I think one really has to differentiate here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But their legal status -- they're not -- they're not a combatant member of one of the three armies, so --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not a combatant member of one of the three armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when talking about cooperation, if we talk about, quickly, in terms of the difference within multinational operations, the Germans and the United States fighting together on the same front, in cooperation, would you tell me that the Germans are criminally responsible for the crimes committed by the United States?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when the Russians defeated the Germans in the Second World War, would you tell me that the Russians would be criminally responsible for the illegal actions of the partisans?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That they were responsible -- the commander was responsible.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, because the partisans were a part -- they were commanded and integrated in the operations by the Stavka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if they were not integrated, then --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were not integrated, but they were even used in -- in a very strategic way in the rear, and I know from my knowledge of the Second World War that they were very closely connected with the ongoing military operations and that the highest command of the Russian -- or the Soviet Armed Forces by that time connected this and there were even key military leaders flown in to -- to command and control these partisan movements, which were on a very large scale. So I think this is, in my opinion, a thing where the Russian command was very much responsible for what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if we move to Iraq, you will agree with me that in Iraq there are many factions fighting with the same goals but there is no link between these forces, in terms of command and control, and that one cannot be said to be responsible for the other one? Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to -- to think it over. I think the -- the army headquarters is responsible for all the actions taken by the armed forces but there are also civil organisations, security organisations involved in what's going on, and they are not responsible for the -- for what they are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when I take -- I would have to give you many examples, but I will -- risk running out of time. But you agree with me, and that was your position yesterday and somewhat today, that to be criminally responsible the forces would have to be under your command during an operation for you to be criminally responsible?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the ideal scenario into planning an operation, as you know it from all your training and your experience, you first you plan an operation and you identify who will attack and where. Would that be a fair --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then you would issue orders for that attack.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again, the ideal situation is you assemble all those who will be part of that attack into what we call an assembly area.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that then you will most likely have training, especially for the leaders around a map like this, where you will play different scenarios and what -- you will do what we call war game the attack?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said in explaining this morning. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then, time allowing, you would even practice actions at the -- at different RV points or actions at the objectives?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Physical practice?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then each hour will come and you would launch the attack.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's the ideal scenario.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in a scenario like this, you know who you're fighting with and who is on your left flank and who is on your right flank.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If unknown elements show up during that attack, towards the end of the attack, and by force they take away from you detainees that you are handling at this time, would that be an indication to you that those forces are fighting together or that that force, kidnapping your own detainees, is a force that is not fighting with you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this individual case is as you just stated, they would not be fighting with me; they would be fighting against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if part of the detainees that were not successfully kidnapped by this other force were placed into a school and guarded against any acts committed by those Mujahedin to protect the civilians, would you say that the Mujahedin and the army are fighting together or that this indicates that on the contrary, they are fighting on different -- not together?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are almost fighting each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if, General, I indicate to you that Mujahedin were using money in all villages trying to recruit people to fight with them for two reasons: One -- because they wanted Muslims to be -- to become fundamentalist and have their own state; and, two, because they were using the pretext that your government is not doing enough, join us and we'll give you $2.000? Are they fighting with or against?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, this is for me now almost hair-splitting, because we all know that the Mujahedin did not come into the country to fight against the Muslims and not to fight against the Bosnian-Herzegovinian army. This is not the reason why they came into the country, just the contrary. And I think we both agree on that one. You just mentioned individual cases, where on a case by case there were clashes with them, but that doesn't mean that they were constantly fighting against each other. We know that they were spearheading their operations and that they're working with the operations. And if a battalion commander tells me the cooperation which we used to have with them really was a key thing for the -- for the morale of my forces, it seems that they cooperated normally in a very smooth way, rather than in a contradictory way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that could be one group, and there were be other elements or other groups --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- that we don't know about.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can't tell either from the documents or your experience --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- about the existence of how many groups there was.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned something about wanting to have some Mujahedin released. And were you given any information about an exchange of prisoners which took place where a commander of the HVO was kidnapped by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You had this information?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you know that when the exchange took place, first a ransom was requested -- an exchange was requested by the Mujahedin themselves.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you know that the Mujahedin did not address -- that they addressed their request for an exchange to the ECMM, the European Community Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that there was at that time all the exchange was organised actually by the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was organised by the ECMM, but I know at least of one case where the 7th Mountain Brigade addressed this particular case to the international commission, asking them to look for the release of soldiers which were Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was before the kidnapping ever took place. This was --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was somewhere I think 14 April, something like this, of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before the actual kidnapping.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. It's not connected --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's not --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- particularly. But you said whether I know of any case. I just said there is at least one case I'm familiar with where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I mention to you, General, that the leading figure of the ECMM in Zenica had a meeting with General Hadzihasanovic and General Hadzihasanovic agreed at that time to secure the place where the exchange took place, he actually positioned his forces there to secure the exchange --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- and agreed that he would fire against the Mujahedin if anything arose, would that be an indication to you that there was cooperation between the Mujahedin and the 3rd Corps or that, on the contrary, there was no cooperation between the two?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is not black/white. In that particular case, you are absolutely right; it seems that General Hadzihasanovic was very -- oh, I don't say that -- he was very angry with the way they did their business, and he was willing to take the actions necessary that they -- that they would convey with his plan of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, a question was put to you whether the 3rd Corps had the necessary forces to take on the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you have no idea what the extent of the Mujahedin problem was.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have no idea. I know this were about a battalion-sized formation broken up in different subunits. And seeing about the size of the 3rd Corps, seeing the security forces, military police forces available, I think there should have been a possibility to do something, because you don't have to fight them all; you just have to fight individuals, especially their leaders, to make them comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, am I right in saying that if you want to attack any force, a minimum ratio of 3 to 1 must be applied to take on a military unit --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is minimum.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So with less than 3 to 1 you can take on a military unit?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the 3 to 1 is a -- is a ratio which sounds nice, but it's not the -- the key figure. And I'll just give you two examples: When -- when the Germans attacked Russia, they were far less than the Russian forces. And if you see that the 1st Armoured Division attacked the Iraq forces with the superiority of the Iraq forces of 10 to 1 against one attacking division, you see the fourth ratio really doesn't say anything in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it is your view that on a small-scale operation -- not a small-scale but an immediate operation, if I want to take a company line I don't need three times the men? Is that what you're saying? Because that's my specific question. If I attack a specific battalion, I put it to you that I need at least three battalions to take on this position.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it really is very hypothetical thing, and we both know that, because it depends on the situation. If the whole battalion is in defence -- I'm attacking, then I would say I need more than one battalion to attack them. I need also artillery. I need other things to do that. That's true. I just want to -- I just want to give away -- get away from this 1 to 3 ratio, because again that doesn't normally say much. This is very academic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can see that time is running out. I need another 15 minutes to ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Make a selection of your questions and only ask the most important ones, because Mr. Dixon needs to ask questions, as well as the Prosecution, and we shouldn't be working after 1.45, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, how much more time may I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five minutes for you; five minutes for Mr. Dixon; and five minutes for the Prosecution. And by that time, it will already be 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I have no time left. It's unfortunate. I would have many questions to put to you arising from the questions of the Judges, but I don't have the time and I cannot do it. I think it's very unfortunate, but I have just a couple -- a few questions. You mentioned the name of Siber today. Now, I'd like to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session. It is necessary for this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You are aware, General, of a situation, a scandal which is now ongoing where British forces and American forces have been mistreating prisoners that they took in Iraq - and "mistreating" is a light word for what we see in the papers - are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware, but I would say they are not all prisoners, because most of them are civilians being detained and not military prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that if I propose to you that the commander of the corps who was there today in Iraq, that he probably had no knowledge that this was going on until it hit the paper?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that this is not the case, because he himself has started investigation, having got information, and he has started investigation already a long time ago, and therefore I think what you just have alluded to is not the reality. General Sanchez started as soon as he had got some information on that, but it might have been too late already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you understand, General, that when we talk about the best forces in the world, the German forces, the British forces, the American forces, that things like that are very likely to happen and that it is very difficult for any commander, especially at the corps level, to be aware of what's going on in detention facilities down on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is difficult. I know this from my own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your own experience, General, there was a report that was made by Amnesty International that was -- a letter was sent to you when you were a commander of KFOR, and this letter was saying that there was allegations that people under your command were mistreating detainees. Do you recall this letter being sent to you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall this letter, and I started investigation right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before that letter, you knew nothing about these events.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it also turned out that the allegations were wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dixon, you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, we have no further questions for General Reinhardt in addition to the ones that we've asked already in our cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has just a few additional questions arising from questions put either by the Bench or by my learned colleague for Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General Reinhardt, with respect to detained persons, whether prisoners of war or civilians, His Honour Judge Swart asked a number of questions concerning detention facilities. My question is: Based on your experience or knowledge, what branch or -- or military subspecialty would you expect to be directly involved for the handling, security, and treatment of prisoners of war or civilians who fall into the hands of the military?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the best ones to take care of the prisoners of war should be military police forces to do the first handling, but we know that there are scarce resources and therefore it's most of the time not only military police but it's also regular forces who have to do that, and therefore it's even more important to transfer them into civil detention facilities as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, in response to a question from His Honour the Presiding Judge, you told us how important professionalism was at the company or platoon level.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I believe you said that that was perhaps even more important than at the high brass level. And if I recall, you also said that if soldiers didn't have confidence in company or platoon leaders, that they "probably wouldn't leave the trench."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on the documents and other information that you possess Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with respect to events in Central Bosnia in 1993, did ABiH soldiers in fact leave the trenches?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are quite a few indications that ABiH soldiers just went home and did not continue, and this was one of the big problems for the commanders, that their soldier just left the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: General, I understand that this was a problem, but did in fact soldiers of the ABiH engage the HVO during the period in 1993 in combat?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Also in response to questions by His Honour Judge Antonetti, you mentioned partisan warfare for defence. Now, I understand that this might be something that you're not familiar with. And if -- if that's the case, please tell us. But what is your understanding of the former JNA or former Yugoslav concept of partisan warfare? What does that entail? What is it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a -- a defence -- a local defence of territorial forces, a prepared defence which basically is responsible for, as I said, the local defence. In addition to those partisan kind of territorial defence, the Yugoslav army had operational forces that could reinforce the Territorial Defence, who could also create main thrusts in some area. So there is a network of soldiers in the territorial defence all over the country. And in addition, you have this mobile defence or mobile operational forces who could reinforce and work with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Reinhardt. That completes the Prosecution's examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Reinhardt, this brings your hearing to an end. We'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague. We know that spending five days here and having to answer questions continually is something you are not used to. We'd like to thank you for your cooperation and your contribution to the determination of the truth. We know you are a very busy person, and we would like to thank you yet again for having testified here. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to Mr. Withopf. But before I do so, there are two issues I would like to address: The first one concerns the question of documents, which was raised this morning. We mentioned this issue during the break, and we think that it would be best if the Prosecution and the Defence reached an agreement with regard to what should be done with this document. Because the situation such as you have presented it means that the Defence has presented documents to be marked for identification, but the Prosecution would like a final exhibit number to be given to these documents. They don't want a DH number to be given to these documents but a P number, and this might give the impression that the Prosecution provided these documents; whereas, the documents come from the Defence. Try to sort this problem out. Discuss the matter. And next week we will see what we should do with the documents from 153 to 164. That was the first point. We have a programme -- a schedule that we should be following next week. That was the second point I wanted to address. Mr. Withopf, I think that perhaps you wanted to comment on this. Please take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, that's exactly the case. I wish to address a number of issues related to the next week's schedule, and for that purpose could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of May, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.03 p.m.,
